summary.text: For each bound \(B\), only finitely many pairs \((p,q)\) with \(p\) prime, \(q>0\), and \(\phi(p)\phi(q)\le B\) exist: \(\phi(p)=p-1\) bounds \(p\), while bounded totient bounds both the prime divisors and their exponents in \(q\). Choosing \(n>2\) outside the finite set of sums of such pairs, the assumed positivity supplies a decomposition with \(x=\phi(p)\phi(q)\) and prime \(x^4+1\); if this prime were at most \(B\), then \(x\le x^4+1\le B\), contradicting the choice of \(n\), so such primes are arbitrarily large.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\phi\) denote Euler's totient function, and define
\[
a(n)=\#\bigl\{p<n: p\text{ is prime and }(\phi(p)\phi(n-p))^4+1\text{ is prime}\bigr\}.
\]
Because \(p<n\), the integer \(q=n-p\) occurring here is automatically positive. Assume the conjectured positivity statement
\[
 a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every }n>2.
\]
We prove that there are infinitely many primes of the form \(x^4+1\).

We first establish the finiteness fact about Euler's totient function that will be needed in the main argument.

**Lemma.** For each fixed nonnegative integer \(K\), there are only finitely many nonnegative integers \(m\) satisfying \(\phi(m)\le K\).

**Proof of the lemma.** We use the standard elementary divisibility property
\[
 d\mid m\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \phi(d)\mid\phi(m).
\]
This property can be seen directly from prime factorizations. If
\(d=\prod_p p^{a_p}\) and \(m=\prod_p p^{b_p}\), with \(0\le a_p\le b_p\), then for every \(a_p>0\),
\[
 \phi(p^{a_p})=p^{a_p-1}(p-1)
 \quad\text{divides}\quad
 \phi(p^{b_p})=p^{b_p-1}(p-1),
\]
and the multiplicative prime-power formulas for the two totients give the asserted divisibility. Prime powers occurring only in \(m\) simply contribute additional integral factors to \(\phi(m)\).

Suppose now that \(m>0\) and \(\phi(m)\le K\). Let \(p\) be any prime divisor of \(m\), and let \(e\ge1\) be the exponent of \(p\) in the prime factorization of \(m\). Since \(p\mid m\), the divisibility property gives \(\phi(p)\mid\phi(m)\). Both quantities are positive, so
\[
 p-1=\phi(p)\le\phi(m)\le K.
\]
Consequently
\[
 p\le K+1. \tag{1}
\]
Likewise \(p^e\mid m\), so \(\phi(p^e)\mid\phi(m)\), and hence
\[
 p^{e-1}(p-1)=\phi(p^e)\le K.
\]
As \(p-1\ge1\), this implies
\[
 p^{e-1}\le K. \tag{2}
\]
In particular, the exponent \(e\) is bounded in terms of \(K\). A convenient coarse bound is
\[
 e\le K+1. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, if \(e>K+1\), then \(e>K\). Since \(p\ge2\),
\[
 p^{e-1}\ge 2^{e-1}\ge e>K;
\]
here \(2^{e-1}\ge e\) for \(e\ge1\), as follows immediately by induction. This contradicts (2).

It follows from (1) and (3) that every prime-power factor of \(m\) obeys
\[
 p^e\le (K+1)^{K+1}. \tag{4}
\]
Moreover, all distinct prime divisors of \(m\) lie among the integers \(0,1,\ldots,K+1\), so their number is at most \(K+2\). Multiplying the estimates (4) over the distinct prime factors in the factorization of \(m\), we obtain the coarse uniform bound
\[
 m\le \bigl((K+1)^{K+1}\bigr)^{K+2}
   =(K+1)^{(K+1)(K+2)}. \tag{5}
\]
The exceptional nonpositive case in the natural numbers is just \(m=0\), which is also contained in a finite initial interval. Thus every \(m\) with \(\phi(m)\le K\) belongs to a fixed finite initial interval depending only on \(K\). This proves the lemma. \(\square\)

We now prove the desired infinitude. It is enough to prove that primes of the required form are unbounded: a finite set of natural numbers has a largest element, or at least an upper bound, so an unbounded set cannot be finite.

Fix an arbitrary nonnegative integer \(B\). We shall construct a prime \(r>B\) of the form \(x^4+1\).

Consider all ordered pairs \((p,q)\) satisfying
\[
 p\text{ is prime},\qquad q>0,\qquad \phi(p)\phi(q)\le B. \tag{6}
\]
Call these the bad pairs for the bound \(B\). There are only finitely many such pairs. To see this, first note that \(q>0\) implies \(\phi(q)>0\), hence \(\phi(q)\ge1\). Therefore (6) gives
\[
 \phi(p)\le \phi(p)\phi(q)\le B.
\]
Since \(p\) is prime, \(\phi(p)=p-1\), and consequently
\[
 p\le B+1. \tag{7}
\]
Thus there are only finitely many possibilities for \(p\). Also a prime \(p\) is positive, so \(\phi(p)=p-1>0\) and in particular \(\phi(p)\ge1\). Hence (6) also yields
\[
 \phi(q)\le \phi(p)\phi(q)\le B. \tag{8}
\]
By the lemma, there are only finitely many possible \(q\) satisfying (8). Combining this with (7), the collection of bad pairs is finite.

It follows that the corresponding set of bad sums
\[
 \mathcal S_B= igl\{p+q:(p,q)\text{ is a bad pair for }B\bigr\}
\]
is finite. Choose an integer \(C\) that is at least every element of \(\mathcal S_B\). If \(\mathcal S_B\) is empty, any nonnegative \(C\), for example \(0\), will do. Set
\[
 n=\max\{C+1,3\}.
\]
Then \(n>2\), and \(n\notin\mathcal S_B\): indeed, \(n\ge C+1>C\), whereas every member of \(\mathcal S_B\) is at most \(C\).

Apply the assumed positivity conjecture to this \(n\). Since \(a(n)>0\), the set counted by \(a(n)\) is nonempty. Hence there is an integer \(p<n\) such that
\[
 p\text{ is prime}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \bigl(\phi(p)\phi(n-p)\bigr)^4+1\text{ is prime}. \tag{9}
\]
Put
\[
 q=n-p,
 \qquad
 x=\phi(p)\phi(q),
 \qquad
 r=x^4+1.
\]
Because \(p<n\), we have \(q>0\), and also
\[
 p+q=p+(n-p)=n. \tag{10}
\]
By (9), \(r\) is prime, and by its definition it is of the desired form \(x^4+1\).

It remains to show that \(r>B\). Suppose, to the contrary, that \(r\le B\). For every nonnegative integer \(x\),
\[
 x\le x^4+1.
\]
For \(x=0\) this is immediate; for \(x\ge1\), one has \(x\le x^4\), and hence certainly \(x\le x^4+1\). Therefore
\[
 \phi(p)\phi(q)=x\le r\le B. \tag{11}
\]
Together with the facts that \(p\) is prime and \(q>0\), (11) says precisely that \((p,q)\) is a bad pair. Its sum \(p+q\) must consequently belong to \(\mathcal S_B\). But (10) says this sum is \(n\), while \(n\) was deliberately chosen not to belong to \(\mathcal S_B\). This contradiction proves that
\[
 r>B.
\]

Thus, for every proposed bound \(B\), there exists a prime \(r>B\) and an integer \(x\ge0\) such that \(r=x^4+1\). The set of primes of the form \(x^4+1\) is therefore unbounded in the natural numbers. Since every finite set of natural numbers is bounded, this set is infinite, as required.
